evidence: Juv. 5.68: solidae jam mūcida frusta farīnae
Juv. 14.128: mūcida caeruleī pānis cōnsūmere frusta
terms.comment: Of bread and wine gone mouldy or musty, in Juvenal and Martial. In Plautus the word means “snivelling” (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Col. 12.4.4: nē sitū penora mūcōrem contrahant
terms.comment: To go mouldy is mūcōrem contrahere, Columella’s phrase for stored food and vinegar. His situs is the staleness of things left standing too long.

evidence: Cato Agr. 148: quod neque aceat neque mūceat
Plin. NH 14.131: proprium est vīnō mūcēscere (Lewis & Short)

phrases.english: The bread is mouldy; throw it away.
The strawberries have gone mouldy; let’s throw them out.

phrases.latin: neque enim omnia sustinet umquam mūcida caeruleī pānis cōnsūmere frusta
phrases.english: for he can never bring himself to finish up all the mouldy crusts of blue-grey bread

phrases.latin: locum esse dēbēre āversum ā sōle, quam frīgidissimum et siccissimum, nē sitū penora mūcōrem contrahant
phrases.english: the place should face away from the sun and be as cold and dry as possible, so that the provisions do not go stale and mouldy

sources: Lewis & Short: mucidus · Lewis & Short: mucor · Lewis & Short: muceo · Lewis & Short: mucesco
